title: Document how to keep token cost controllable as a project's decision history grows
detail:
AUTONOMOUS: yes.

WHY THIS IS A PRODUCT DELIVERABLE, not internal notes: keeping token cost
controllable over long time and much growth is a Shipwright feature claim. The
measurement that produced these cards (187 sessions, 54,516 API calls) also
produced the operator-side answers, and none of them can ship as a DEFAULT —
`autoCompactWindow` and the effort level are Claude Code user settings a plugin
cannot set, and pinning a model tier would move a consuming project's bill
without their consent. Advice is the correct shipping vehicle: a document can
recommend and explain without coercing.

DELIVER:
1. A new page under `docs/` — working title "Handling a large decision history"
   (or "Keeping token cost controllable"). Contents, all measured:
   - The cost equation: cost = calls x context. Every API call re-pays the whole
     accumulated context; cache reads were 82% of the measured bill. 78.1% of
     calls added under 2k tokens yet accounted for 80.6% of cost.
   - Set an auto-compact window. Measured: a median iterate runs 73k -> 508k of
     context; capping it held the maximum at 366k. Why 400k rather than 200k for
     a stateful pipeline: the first compaction must not land in the phase where
     state still exists only in the conversation.
   - Effort level: output per call fell from a median of 500 to 350 tokens.
     Hidden thinking was 43.9% of context growth, the single largest driver, and
     it persists across turns on current models.
   - A cheaper model for building, a stronger one for reviewing — as SUBAGENTS,
     never a mid-session switch, because the model is part of the prompt-cache
     key. Measured: 3x lower weighted token load at identical raw token volume;
     internal reviewers cost $2-5.50 each and are worth it.
   - What is NOT the problem, so readers do not chase it: the decision log and
     the event log are ~0% of measured cost. Falsified explicitly, because the
     intuition that they drive cost is strong and wrong.
   - How to see your own numbers, once the context-cost meter is available.
2. `docs/guide.md` updates: Chapter 8 (quality gates) gains the cost dimension,
   Appendix B gains the meter and readiness commands, and the phases chapter
   notes where review model choice applies.
3. `README.md` gets one line pointing at the new page, per its summary-plus-link
   role.

FRAME IT AS ADVICE WITH MEASURED NUMBERS AND STATED LIMITS, not as settings to
copy blindly: the 43.9% thinking share is a function of one effort level on one
repo and will differ elsewhere. Say so, so a reader can tell which numbers
transfer and which do not.

Depends on the meter being live (PR #591 merged but the plugin cache was never
synced, so it has produced zero data so far) — the document should tell readers
how to measure, not only what we measured.

title: Stop ignoring the decision-drops folder in three places, including the template every adopted project gets
detail:
AUTONOMOUS: yes.

Re-filed to add the third location, which the earlier version missed: fixing only
this repo would leave every future project with the same defect.

THE PROBLEM. Every change writes a note saying why it was decided that way, into
`.shipwright/agent_docs/decision-drops/`. Those notes are filed into the archive
(`decision_log.md`) only by `/shipwright-changelog` Step 4 — a RELEASE. Measured
on main 2026-08-07: 202 notes waiting, and `decision_log.md` last written
2026-07-20. The folder is gitignored on the premise that the notes are
short-lived. At the current release cadence they are not: ten weeks of
architectural decisions exist on exactly one machine, absent from CI, absent from
any second checkout, and lost with the disk.

AGGREGATION STAYS WHERE IT IS. `/shipwright-changelog` Step 4 is the one
serialized, lock-held point that assigns the sequential `ADR-NNN`. Moving it
reintroduces the numbering race. The durability problem gets solved on the other
side instead.

THREE PLACES, not one:
1. This repo: `.gitignore:172` — `/.shipwright/agent_docs/decision-drops/`.
2. **`shared/templates/shipwright-gitignore.template:45`** — the same rule, and
   this is what every onboarded project receives. Without this, adopt keeps
   creating projects with the defect built in. Check
   `plugins/shipwright-adopt/scripts/lib/gitignore_check.py` too: if it asserts
   the rule is present, it will fight the change.
3. The shipwright-webui repo — same rule, same exposure, separate repo.

THEN: Layer-1 context loading reads the drops as well as `decision_log.md`. Today
it reads neither the drops (they were invisible) nor, in practice, the full log.
Without this step, tracking the folder fixes durability but not the ten-week
blind spot in what agents actually see.

ALSO re-verify, because tracking changes both: that drop-dir consumers still
resolve against the MAIN repo root rather than a worktree
(`test_decision_drop_ssot.py` guards this in both directions), and what
`git worktree remove` and `git add -A` will now sweep.

NOTE: this deliberately reverses the earlier "the gitignore is correct, do not
revert" decision recorded in the launch-prep plan. Its premise — that drops are
short-lived — is measurably false at the current release cadence, and the
alternative fix would cost the serialized numbering. Operator decision,
2026-08-07. Related: `trg-e21cc409` was marked resolvable-on-merge 79 days ago
and is still open; likely stale, GC candidate.

title: Extend the ADR index to the two collections without one, and fix the trigger and merge shape it is missing today
detail:
AUTONOMOUS: yes. Absorbs trg-386bd01c and trg-1acb5304.

Re-filed after the operator asked the right question: how does the index stay
correct for all three collections, cleanly wired and enforced? Checked — TODAY IT
IS NOT, and two open cards already prove it. Extending the producer without
fixing those would spread a known breakage to two more collections.

WHAT EXISTS. `.shipwright/planning/adr/INDEX.md` (57 lines / 6.7 KB over 52 ADR
spec files) is auto-generated by `shared/scripts/tools/rebuild_adr_index.py`, with
a lock and a churn register, behind ADR-116/ADR-120. Two collections have NO
index: `decision_log.md` (333 entries / 570 KB) and the decision drops (202).

MEASURED VALUE. 328 decisions as an index = 6,891 tokens; 202 drops = 4,085;
together 10,977 tokens against 276,183 to read them in full. 25x compression.
This is what turns "read all decisions" from an instruction nobody can follow
into one that is actually followable.

THREE DEFECTS TO CLOSE TOGETHER:
1. EXTEND: give the two unindexed collections the same generated index, from the
   same producer.
2. TRIGGER (trg-386bd01c, absorbed): `rebuild_adr_index()` is called only inside
   `aggregate_decisions.py`'s `if valid:` branch — i.e. only as a side effect of
   folding drops. An ADR written straight to `.shipwright/planning/adr/` never
   reaches the index until some later release happens to have drops. Evidence:
   webui's INDEX.md sat at ADR-133 while 134-138 were unlisted. Regenerate when a
   decision file changes, not when drops are folded.
3. MERGE SHAPE (trg-1acb5304, absorbed): the index is regenerated on a BRANCH at
   F3, so two parallel iterates each append a row at the same anchor — a 3-way
   conflict. INDEX.md is not in `CHURN_ALLOWLIST` and has no `merge=union`
   `.gitattributes` entry, so `resolve_churn_conflicts` calls it blocking and
   `ensure_current` aborts. Fails safely but needs a human every time. Add it to
   the allowlist and keep the documented SSoT in sync
   (`test_churn_merge_doc_sync`).

ENFORCEMENT — the answer to "how does it stay correct": a drift test that
REGENERATES and COMPARES, following the `gate_catalog.json` + `gate_catalog.md`
pattern this repo already uses, and keeping the generated file next to the source
it comes from so the test has an obvious subject. There is no such guard for this
catalogue today, which is why drift went unnoticed.

Two schemas worth copying rather than inventing: Claude Code's `MEMORY.md`
enforces its index cap at WRITE time with an error and rewrites to 70% of cap;
the IETF RFC index carries bidirectional `obsoletes` / `obsoleted-by` with
`current-status` DERIVED from the link graph — the only correct approach when 328
decisions carry just 16 `Status` fields.

RELATION TO THE CONTEXT-REGISTER CARD (trg-c7ef6eac): different artifact, and NOT
a hard dependency — an earlier version of this card overstated that. A plain
table of contents delivers the compression on its own. The register is what later
allows filtering it by relevance ("which decisions touch this area"). Ship this
first; the register makes it smarter.

Fold in trg-3a4c6a3d (agents inline full ADR rationale instead of a terse
index) — same idea, smaller scope.

title: Document the strategies for keeping token cost controllable, organised by when a project needs them
detail:
AUTONOMOUS: yes.

Re-filed on operator direction: this must NOT read as a report of what we
measured. It is a how-to, organised by THRESHOLD -> STRATEGY. A reader should be
able to look up their own situation ("I have this many iterates, my decision
history is this big") and find the two or three things worth doing, without
reading any analysis.

SHAPE — for each threshold, name the observable trigger, the symptom, and the
action. Draft thresholds (derived from this repo's shape at ~1.7 KB per decision
entry; state that assumption so a reader can adjust, and verify before shipping):

  ~20+ iterates / decision history over ~35 KB
    -> Set an auto-compact window before it starts to matter. Explain the
       trade-off in one line: compacting earlier is cheaper but the first
       compaction must not land in a phase whose state is still only in the
       conversation.

  ~35+ iterates / decision history over ~100 KB
    -> The history is now a measurable share of EVERY session, because it is
       still small enough to be read in full. This is the band where an index
       starts paying for itself.

  ~90+ iterates / decision history over ~2,000 lines
    -> It has silently stopped being read at all — one read returns at most
       2,000 lines. Switch to index-plus-detail-on-demand; a "read it all"
       instruction is no longer being followed regardless of what it says.

  Sessions running long (a few hundred exchanges)
    -> Lower the reasoning effort level; use a cheaper model for building and a
       stronger one for reviewing, as SUBAGENTS — never a mid-session switch,
       because the model is part of the prompt cache and switching re-pays the
       whole context.

  Any size
    -> What is NOT worth optimising, stated plainly so nobody spends a week on
       it: the decision log and the event log are not what makes sessions
       expensive. Cost tracks the NUMBER of exchanges times how much context each
       one carries.

RULES FOR THE WRITING:
1. Recommendations, never shipped defaults. The auto-compact window and the
   effort level are Claude Code user settings a plugin cannot set, and choosing a
   model tier for a consuming project moves their bill without consent. A
   document can advise without coercing — that is why this is the right vehicle.
2. Numbers only where they define a threshold or a trade-off. No attribution
   tables, no percentages of our own bill, no methodology.
3. Say which numbers are specific to this repo and which transfer.
4. Point at the meter for "measure your own", rather than substituting our
   figures for theirs.

DELIVER: a new page under `docs/` (working title "Keeping token cost
controllable"); `docs/guide.md` updates (Chapter 8 quality gates gains the cost
dimension, Appendix B gains the meter and readiness commands); one line in
`README.md` per its summary-plus-link role.

role, sets the precedence (flag > project config > unset), and its REJECTED
section already carries the consumer-freedom argument against pinning a tier.
This card is the separate defect underneath it: **a role in the registry that no
skill calls.** Tiering an agent that is never spawned changes nothing.

VERIFIED 2026-08-07 by a full grep over plugins/ (.md and .py, worktrees
excluded): `opus-plan-reviewer` is referenced by NO file except itself. Its own
frontmatter advertises "fallback when external LLM review is unavailable", but
`/shipwright-plan` Step 5 has three branches and none reach it:
  - external available  -> `external_review.py --mode plan`
  - no API key          -> interactive retry-or-skip -> Self-Review Fallback
  - user disabled       -> Self-Review Fallback
The Self-Review Fallback is a 5-item checklist ("2x denken") worked through by
THE SAME AGENT THAT WROTE THE PLAN. So when external review is unavailable, the
plan gate degrades to self-assessment.

THE ASYMMETRY: code review at medium+ has an internal cascade
(spec -> code -> doubt) PLUS a mandatory external pass. Plan review has external
only. Nothing designed that.

opinion: the internal reviewer can read the repo; the external providers only see
the text they are sent. Measured in iterate-2026-08-07-test-phase-attribution,
where the internal plan review ran only because the operator ordered it, ran
FIRST, and found two BUILD-BLOCKING findings the external pass did not:
  - an attempt-counter collision across the CPU-lease window (the multi-hour
    queueing that iterate exists to measure)
  - `run_test_suite.py` at 518 lines against a cap of 300 (zero headroom), which
    forced a different design

check. The external pass then found two further highs on the revised spec.
Neither was redundant — consistent with the measured result that the internal
cascade caught 21 items external review missed (#438).

1. Wire the plan-reviewer into `/shipwright-plan` Step 5 at medium+, before the
   external pass, and let it carry the pass on the two branches where external

title: TC2.1 (auto) Fill the context-index selection keys from the sources that already hold them, and declare the one that has none
detail:
AUTONOMOUS: yes.

LANDMINE: `.shipwright/runtime/events-context-index.json` has 815 entries and the
right envelope with content-hash invalidation — but the SELECTION KEYS ARE EMPTY:
`area_ids` 23%, `changed_files` 23%, `affected_frs` 13%, `commit` 9%,
`supersedes` 4%, and `extraction.confidence: "low"` on 630 of 815. THERE IS
NOTHING TO RANK. Any relevance ordering built on this today is fiction. The cause
is that the keys were meant to come from LLM extraction, which produced low
confidence and then nothing usable.

CHECKED KEY BY KEY 2026-08-07 — four of five are recoverable from producers that
already exist, and no LLM is needed for any of them:
  - `commit`, `changed_files` -> git, trivially.
  - `area_ids` -> git plus the area catalogue. All 28 entries in
    `.shipwright/agent_docs/area_catalog.json` are `source: "deterministic"` and
    every one carries `path_patterns` (e.g. `CHANGELOG-unreleased.d/**`). Match a
    commit's changed files against those patterns and the area ids follow as a
    pure function of git.
  - `affected_frs` -> THE EVENT LOG, not git. The FR gate enforces this field at
    F11, so it is already recorded per run: measured 484 events carrying the gate
    fields, 108 with a non-empty `affected_frs` (1-16 FRs each). The other 376
    carry `change_type` instead, which is the legal no-FR branch — a DECLARED
    absence, not a gap. `fr_history.py` already queries this direction
    ("which recorded changes touched a requirement"), so the join exists and is
    proven.
  - `supersedes` -> the only genuinely missing input. Needs an explicit
    declaration, or derivation from the ADR link graph (the RFC-index pattern in
    the ADR-index card: `current-status` derived from `obsoletes` /
    `obsoleted-by`, which is the only correct approach when 328 ADRs carry just
    16 `Status` fields).

SCOPE:
1. Backfill `commit`, `changed_files`, `area_ids` from git and the area
   catalogue; backfill `affected_frs` from the event log. Deterministic and
   re-runnable — running it twice must produce the same index.
2. Keep them filled with `ADR:` / `Area:` / `FR:` commit trailers, with the area
   value verified against the catalogue rather than hand-typed.
3. Record per entry which keys are DERIVED, which are DECLARED (the
   `change_type` case), and which are UNAVAILABLE. Coverage belongs in the
   ENVELOPE as well as per row — a per-row flag cannot report an absent row.
4. Drop the low-confidence extraction path rather than leaving it beside the
   deterministic one, or the two will disagree and nobody will know which won.

This is the precondition for the ADR-index card: nothing can be ranked by
relevance until the keys exist.

title: TC3.1 (auto, serial 1/3) Stop ignoring the decision-drops folder in three places, including the template every adopted project gets
detail:
AUTONOMOUS: yes.

this repo would leave every future project with the same defect.

THE PROBLEM. Every change writes a note saying why it was decided that way, into
`.shipwright/agent_docs/decision-drops/`. Those notes are filed into the archive
(`decision_log.md`) only by `/shipwright-changelog` Step 4 — a RELEASE. Measured
on main 2026-08-07: 202 notes waiting, and `decision_log.md` last written
2026-07-20. The folder is gitignored on the premise that the notes are
short-lived. At the current release cadence they are not: ten weeks of
architectural decisions exist on exactly one machine, absent from CI, absent from
any second checkout, and lost with the disk.

AGGREGATION STAYS WHERE IT IS. `/shipwright-changelog` Step 4 is the one
serialized, lock-held point that assigns the sequential `ADR-NNN`. Moving it
reintroduces the numbering race. The durability problem gets solved on the other
side instead.

THREE PLACES, not one:
1. This repo: `.gitignore:172` — `/.shipwright/agent_docs/decision-drops/`.
2. **`shared/templates/shipwright-gitignore.template:45`** — the same rule, and
   this is what every onboarded project receives. Without this, adopt keeps
   creating projects with the defect built in. Check
   `plugins/shipwright-adopt/scripts/lib/gitignore_check.py` too: if it asserts
   the rule is present, it will fight the change.
3. The shipwright-webui repo — same rule, same exposure, separate repo.

THEN: Layer-1 context loading reads the drops as well as `decision_log.md`. Today
it reads neither the drops (they were invisible) nor, in practice, the full log.
Without this step, tracking the folder fixes durability but not the ten-week
blind spot in what agents actually see.

ALSO re-verify, because tracking changes both: that drop-dir consumers still
resolve against the MAIN repo root rather than a worktree
(`test_decision_drop_ssot.py` guards this in both directions), and what
`git worktree remove` and `git add -A` will now sweep.

revert" decision recorded in the launch-prep plan. Its premise — that drops are
short-lived — is measurably false at the current release cadence, and the
alternative fix would cost the serialized numbering. Operator decision,

title: TC3.2 (auto, serial 2/3) A truncated mandated context load is never reported, so the governance guarantee voids itself silently as a project grows
detail:
AUTONOMOUS: yes. Small — a check, not an architecture.

WHAT "MANDATED LOAD" MEANS: `references/context-loading.md` instructs an iterate
to read certain artifacts COMPLETELY at startup — Layer 1 includes
"`decision_log.md` — ALL architectural decisions (read completely)". That is a
governance promise: the agent is supposed to know every prior decision before
changing anything.

WHY IT SILENTLY STOPS BEING TRUE: `Read` returns at most 2,000 lines.
`decision_log.md` is 4,379 lines. So the agent is told to read the whole file,
receives roughly half, and NOTHING REPORTS THE SHORTFALL — it just proceeds,
usually falling back to greps. Measured across four projects 2026-08-07:
  leadwright        23 KB /   450 lines -> read in full   (1 of 1 sessions)
  shipwright       570 KB / 4,379 lines -> fragments      (15 of 194)
  shipwright-webui 641 KB                -> fragments      (6 of 85)
The guarantee holds while a project is small and evaporates exactly when the
project is mature enough to need it.

THIS IS NOT A COST FIX. The two big logs are ~0% of measured token cost; the
earlier claim that they drive it is falsified. This card is about correctness of
the product promise.

SCOPE: when a mandated load is truncated, say so — name the artifact, how much
arrived, how much exists, and that the instruction was not fulfilled. More
generally, any projection must DECLARE ITS COVERAGE so "I could not fit it all"
becomes a reported fact rather than a silent one. `event_context.py query`
already does this correctly and is the template.

The dangerous band is ~100-260 KB: still under the line cap, so still read in
full, already 6-13% of a session's context.

title: TC4.1 (auto, last) Document the strategies for keeping token cost controllable, organised by when a project needs them
detail:
AUTONOMOUS: yes.

Re-filed on operator direction: this must NOT read as a report of what we
measured. It is a how-to, organised by THRESHOLD -> STRATEGY. A reader should be
able to look up their own situation ("I have this many iterates, my decision
history is this big") and find the two or three things worth doing, without
reading any analysis.

SHAPE — for each threshold, name the observable trigger, the symptom, and the
action. Draft thresholds (derived from this repo's shape at ~1.7 KB per decision
entry; state that assumption so a reader can adjust, and verify before shipping):

  ~20+ iterates / decision history over ~35 KB
    -> Set an auto-compact window before it starts to matter. Explain the
       trade-off in one line: compacting earlier is cheaper but the first
       compaction must not land in a phase whose state is still only in the
       conversation.

  ~35+ iterates / decision history over ~100 KB
    -> The history is now a measurable share of EVERY session, because it is
       still small enough to be read in full. This is the band where an index
       starts paying for itself.

  ~90+ iterates / decision history over ~2,000 lines
    -> It has silently stopped being read at all — one read returns at most
       2,000 lines. Switch to index-plus-detail-on-demand; a "read it all"
       instruction is no longer being followed regardless of what it says.

  Sessions running long (a few hundred exchanges)
    -> Lower the reasoning effort level; use a cheaper model for building and a
       stronger one for reviewing, as SUBAGENTS — never a mid-session switch,
       because the model is part of the prompt cache and switching re-pays the
       whole context.

  Any size
    -> What is NOT worth optimising, stated plainly so nobody spends a week on
       it: the decision log and the event log are not what makes sessions
       expensive. Cost tracks the NUMBER of exchanges times how much context each
       one carries.

RULES FOR THE WRITING:
1. Recommendations, never shipped defaults. The auto-compact window and the
   effort level are Claude Code user settings a plugin cannot set, and choosing a
   model tier for a consuming project moves their bill without consent. A
   document can advise without coercing — that is why this is the right vehicle.
2. Numbers only where they define a threshold or a trade-off. No attribution
   tables, no percentages of our own bill, no methodology.
3. Say which numbers are specific to this repo and which transfer.
4. Point at the meter for "measure your own", rather than substituting our
   figures for theirs.

DELIVER: a new page under `docs/` (working title "Keeping token cost
controllable"); `docs/guide.md` updates (Chapter 8 quality gates gains the cost
dimension, Appendix B gains the meter and readiness commands); one line in
`README.md` per its summary-plus-link role.

title: P2.46 [GUIDED] Add an `amend` event so a card can be corrected without being dismissed and re-filed
detail:
OPERATOR OBSERVATION, 2026-08-07: "wir editieren wirklich viiiiieeeelll". Correct, and measurable.

THE COST, MEASURED IN THIS SESSION. Over 2026-08-05/07 roughly 30 cards were dismissed and re-filed for no reason other than a changed title, a corrected mode tag, or an added sequencing note. Content was identical in almost every case. Each one costs two events, a new id, and a broken cross-reference; several cards on the board now carry two or three superseded ancestors that say nothing but "retitled". One re-file wave alone was 23 cards / 46 events, and it happened on a premise that later turned out wrong - so the churn was pure loss.

WHY APPEND-ONLY IS NOT THE MISTAKE. The store is git-tracked with merge=union plus a triage-specific dedup, and that is precisely what let ~12 concurrent worktrees write to it this week without a single conflict. A mutable file would reintroduce the N(N-1)/2 collision class that DERIVED_SNAPSHOTS exists to prevent. Append-only buys parallelism; it is load-bearing and must stay.

THE SHAPE THAT KEEPS BOTH. A third event type alongside `append` and `status`:

    {"event":"amend","id":"trg-x","title":"...","detail":"...","by":"...","ts":"..."}

Applied by the reader in the same second pass that already applies `status`, ordered by (ts, file-order) exactly like status flips are today. Fields absent from the amend are left untouched, so a title-only correction is a title-only amend.

WHAT IT BUYS:
  * stable ids - correcting a title stops re-minting the card, so cross-references survive;
  * still strictly append-only - union merge stays conflict-free, parallelism is untouched;
  * BETTER history, not worse - today you see "dismissed: retitled as X" and must go find X; an amend shows the change itself, in place;
  * far less dismissal noise - the dismissed pile stops being half bookkeeping.

WHY GUIDED, NOT AUTO - three real decisions, none of which should be made by an autonomous run:
  (a) WHICH FIELDS may be amended. Title and detail are obvious. Severity is arguable. `kind`, `source`, `dedupKey` and `runId` are probably NOT amendable - a card whose dedup key can change breaks idempotent producers. Draw that line explicitly.
  (b) WHO may amend. A human via CLI, certainly. An automated producer amending its own earlier card is attractive (the rolling compliance card would stop churning) but it turns amend into a mutation path for machines and deserves its own thought.
  (c) READERS MUST ALL LEARN IT, or a card reads differently depending on which surface you look at. Known consumers: read_all_items, triage_render, the CLI list/promote/dismiss paths, and the WebUI's own TypeScript reader with its committed parity fixture. A contract bump is required, and the WebUI side is a separate repo - see P2.34, which is exactly this class of cross-repo contract change and is still undecided.

SEQUENCING AND SCOPE HONESTY. This is friction, not data loss - nothing has been lost to it, only time. It should NOT jump the queue ahead of the token-consumption work (TC1-TC4), which is the operator's current priority. File it now so the reasoning is not re-derived later; build it when the surface is being touched anyway.

DO NOT, while here: make the store mutable, rewrite existing append lines, or "compact" the dismissed history. The 30 supersede chains already written stay as they are - they are honest records of what happened.

title: TC3.3 (auto, serial 3/3) Persist the iterate state that currently exists only in the conversation, so a compaction cannot lose work
detail:
AUTONOMOUS: yes.

OBSERVED 2026-08-07, two of two runs: both iterates compacted, one of them DURING
its external review. Compaction is routine now, not hypothetical —
`autoCompactWindow` is 400k (raised from 300k for exactly this reason) and a
median iterate runs 73k -> 508k of context.

WHAT IS AT RISK — the state that has no disk representation today:
  1. Interview answers. The `[interview]` step's questions and answers are never
     written anywhere; they exist only as conversation.
  2. The mini-plan at complexity `small`. At `small` there is no plan file — the
     plan is agreed in conversation and built from memory.
  3. Architecture-review reconciliation. What the review found and what was
     decided about it is conversational; only the outcome eventually shows up in
     a diff.
  4. Review findings between a reviewer returning and `record_review_pass.py`
     being called. This is the window the observed compaction landed in.
  5. The handoff decision itself. When to hand off to a fresh context is a
     heuristic, not a contract, so the receiving agent cannot know what the
     sending one had.
  6. Resume coverage: B1 checks only two markers, so a mid-phase resume cannot
     tell how far the phase actually got.

WHY IT CANNOT BE SOLVED AT COMPACTION TIME: `PreCompact` can only block or
observe — IT CANNOT SHAPE THE SUMMARY. There is no hook that protects a specific
piece of conversation. The state has to be on disk BEFORE the window opens.

SCOPE:
1. Persist (1) and (2) as they are produced.
2. Write review findings to disk as soon as each reviewer returns, before any
   further work — this alone makes a compaction during review harmless.
3. Then run the acceptance test: kill a run mid-phase and prove it resumes from
   artifacts alone, with no conversational memory.

PREREQUISITE FOR: phase-scoped contexts (each phase must be resumable from disk
before it can be moved into its own context), and any unattended iterate. It is
also why a finalization handoff is currently expensive — the fresh context has to
reload everything from scratch.

=== STEP 1 SELF-VERIFICATION — DO THIS BEFORE PLANNING ANYTHING ===

Four of the six items in the list above are UNVERIFIED at the code. They were
compiled from observation, not from a measurement pass. Before writing a plan,
re-derive each one against current origin/main and record the result in the
spec — verified, corrected, or dropped. Do not build from the list as given.

Why this instruction exists, concretely: on 2026-08-06 an anchor was split into
six work cards without re-checking its members. FOUR of the six were already
delivered — the anchor text predated the PR that closed them by one day, and the
operator only found out by starting one and discovering the work was done. The
same failure mode has hit this board three times: a card claiming a registry
entry was missing when it had been added in the very PR that created it; a
count taken over the wrong predicate; and a gate reported as miscalibrated when
its weight was honest.

The rule this encodes: verify the SPECIFIC claim, never its neighbourhood.
"the constant exists" and "the gate fires" are different statements, and the
second is the one a card asserts. Each of those three errors was one grep away
from being caught.

If a point turns out to be already solved, say so in the spec and shrink the
scope rather than implementing it again. A shrunken TC3.3 is a good outcome.

title: Self-heal op-in-progress probes fail OPEN on a git timeout
detail: Found during review of P2.19e (trg-ca82a057). gitignore_selfheal.py and gitattributes_selfheal.py each carry their own op-in-progress probe (merge/rebase/cherry-pick/revert/bisect detection) ahead of a self-heal commit. Their local git wrapper maps a timeout to a plain non-zero returncode, and both loops then treat ANY non-zero as marker-absent (continue / fall through), the inverted direction from lib.main_tree_guards.op_in_progress, which was hardened specifically against this: there a timeout must read as hazard-present (fail closed), not hazard-absent. Both self-heals run in the iterate worktree immediately before the sweep_outbox commit step, so a hung git during setup could let a self-heal commit into a half-finished merge/rebase. Not fixed here (P2.19e is a behavior-preserving predicate-dedup iterate; this is a behavior change, so it needs its own BUG/CHANGE iterate) but should not be silently dropped.

title: Root the phase-quality Stop audit at the run's own worktree, not cwd
detail: iterate-2026-08-08-run-id-lifecycle-fixes fixed already_audited() to re-audit a provisional unresolvable_run_id_skip SKIP once the run's iterate_history ledger entry appears (trg-b36fd844). Verified during that fix: the re-audit trigger can only fire when audit_phase_quality_on_stop.py's project_root resolves to the run's own worktree, because F5c writes the ledger entry into the WORKTREE, not main. audit_phase_quality_on_stop.py resolves project_root via plain lib.project_root.resolve_project_root (env -> cwd -> subdir), with no pointer-based worktree fallback -- unlike context_cost_session.resolve_active_project_root, which checks the per-session run pointer first specifically because a Stop-subprocess's cwd is the MAIN repo even while an iterate runs in a linked worktree (that module's own docstring). In the dominant main-rooted shape, S2/S3/W2/S9/S10 SKIP for the whole run regardless (already documented, harmless) -- but the re-audit trigger this fix added only pays off for a worktree-rooted audit. Fix: have audit_phase_quality_on_stop.py resolve project_root the same pointer-first way context_cost_session.resolve_active_project_root already does, so the ledger-entry-appeared re-audit (and the five guarded checks generally) can evaluate for real during a live run invoked the ordinary way. Scoped out of the original bundle deliberately -- changing project_root resolution for every phase-quality Stop audit is a materially larger blast radius than either lifecycle fix it rides on.

title: P2.48 [AUTO] Text and I/O robustness: three reader/writer sites that assume well-formed input
detail:
BUNDLES trg-acc195bf, P2.44 (trg-e31066d8) and P2.18b (trg-d13da21d). All low, all the same shape - a read or a write that assumes its input is well-formed - and all following patterns already established by delivered work, so none needs a decision.

THE PRECEDENTS TO FOLLOW, not to re-invent: iterate-2026-08-07-triage-dedup-recursion-guard widened two readers for RecursionError; iterate-2026-08-06-gc-decode-parity fixed the triage-log decode seam; PR #564 guarded F0's console against non-cp1252 output. Each of the three below is the same fix at a site those runs did not touch.

--- four best-effort json.loads readers still miss RecursionError (was trg-acc195bf) ---
churn_merge.dedup_event_lines and lib/triage_dedup.py's _parsed_append were widened (iterate-2026-08-07-triage-dedup-recursion-guard) to catch RecursionError from a deeply-nested JSON line, closing a canonical-lock crash. Four other best-effort per-line json.loads readers of the same events log still catch only (JSONDecodeError/ValueError, TypeError) and would raise RecursionError on the identical input class: campaign_status.py, iterate_phase_groups.py, iterate_timings.py, context_cost_core.py. gate_policy.py already lists RecursionError, so the tree's convention is split. None of these run inside the canonical file lock (lower severity than the fixed sites), but the same 'guard best-effort parse boundaries against the documented RecursionError failure mode' rationale applies. Surfaced by Stage-2 code review during iterate-2026-08-07-triage-dedup-recursion-guard; deliberately NOT fixed there to avoid scope creep beyond the card that iterate was scoped to.

--- three subprocess reads decode strictly and can raise on non-UTF-8 (was trg-e31066d8) ---
Same class as the triage-log seam fixed in iterate-2026-08-06-gc-decode-parity, but in call sites that iterate did not touch. Each captures a child process's output with text mode and an explicit utf-8 encoding but no errors= handler, so the decode is STRICT and a single byte that is not valid UTF-8 raises UnicodeDecodeError out of the reader thread rather than degrading. Observed live: the full shared/tests run for that iterate emitted a PytestUnhandledThreadExceptionWarning for byte 0x81, from subprocess._readerthread. The suite still passed (the exception lands in a reader thread, not the assertion path), which is exactly why it has gone unnoticed - it is latent, not loud. Affects lib/pr_blockers.py, tools/watch_pr_delivery.py and one test helper; all three read tool output that can legitimately carry a cp1252 byte on Windows. Direction is a spurious failure or a swallowed read, never data loss. Fix is a one-word change per site (errors='replace' for human-facing text, or surrogateescape where the bytes must round-trip) plus a regression test seeding a non-UTF-8 byte into captured output.

[NUMBERED 2026-08-06 as P2.44. Same class as P2.36 (F0 console, PR #564) and P2.19f (the triage-log decode seam, PR #587), both delivered: a reader that assumes UTF-8 meets real captured bytes. Those two fixed their own surfaces; this names three more. Follow the pattern they set rather than inventing a third convention.]

--- provenance stamp writes an LF line into a CRLF document (was trg-d13da21d) ---
FOUND 2026-08-06 by the Stage-2 code reviewer during iterate-2026-08-05-adopt-derived-evidence-rollout. NOT introduced by that change - pre-existing in shared stamping already used by the release and documents-only-PR paths.

WHAT: compliance_provenance.stamp_fixed_point rewrites the Source-State line with a regex whose replacement ends in a bare LF. The pattern consumes the original line's carriage return as part of its wildcard, so a document checked out or written with CRLF endings ends up with exactly one LF-only line among CRLF lines.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE NOW: the same function is reached by a new third caller that runs on customer repositories, where a CRLF checkout is the normal case rather than the exception. Previously it ran mainly in this monorepo.

MEASURED SCOPE, so it is not over-stated: the reviewer looked for a CI-vs-local divergence in the delivered tests and found none - the banner parser splits on whitespace, the Group E staleness normaliser strips the banner before comparing, git normalises on commit, and the tests read through universal newlines. So nothing is currently red because of it.

WHAT REMAINS: a committed artifact with mixed line endings, which editors and diff tools flag; and with core.safecrlf=true set (not the default) a git add of that file fails outright.

FIX SHAPE: preserve the matched line's own terminator instead of hardcoding one - capture it in the pattern, or re-append the two-character ending when the match had one. Needs a test with a CRLF fixture, and it touches a function two shipping paths already depend on, which is why it was filed rather than folded into the iterate that found it.

[NUMBERED 2026-08-06 as P2.18b. Second tail of P2.18 (adopt-derived-evidence-rollout), alongside P2.18a. Unlike P2.18a this one is AUTO - a line-ending mismatch has one right answer and no blast radius beyond the stamped document. BLOCKED ON P2.18.]

HONEST NOTE ON THE THIRD: the CRLF one is a line-ending defect rather than a decode defect, so it is the loosest member of this bundle. It is here because the operator asked for small items to be combined and it is two lines in an adjacent area - not because it is the same bug.

title: Ride-along: unbounded .shipwright/.cache/stop-triage-inbox-*.claim accumulation
detail:
Found as a ride-along during shipwright-webui iterate-2026-08-08-triage-filters-sort-parked (Triage tab filters/sort/parked rework). Not built there — root cause lives entirely in this monorepo, no vendored copy exists in shipwright-webui.

WHAT: `.shipwright/.cache/stop-triage-inbox-<uuid>.claim` files accumulate unboundedly in every project using the Stop hook (444+ observed in one long-lived project at investigation time). Gitignored, so it is not a delivery/commit problem, but it swamps recursive file search over `.shipwright/.cache/` and grows without bound over a project's lifetime.

ROOT CAUSE: `aggregate_triage_on_stop.py` (shared/scripts/hooks/) only unlinks its claim file on the FAILURE path (the `finally` block only runs when `ok is False`). The success path -- the overwhelming majority of runs -- never cleans up its claim file. The generic `claim_once()` primitive it calls (shared/scripts/lib/event_once.py) also has no TTL sweep as a backstop.

SUGGESTED FIX SHAPE (not prescriptive): either (a) unlink the claim file on the success path too, mirroring the failure-path cleanup, or (b) add a TTL sweep to claim_once() so stale claims self-expire regardless of which caller forgets to clean up -- the latter is more robust since it protects every future claim_once() caller, not just this one.

SCOPE NOTE: a filter/sort feature must not turn into a hook refactor, per the operator's explicit instruction on the originating card -- hence this is filed separately rather than bundled.

title: Decision-drop JSON payloads aren't scanned on the write path
detail: Since iterate-2026-08-08-track-decision-drops, .shipwright/agent_docs/decision-drops/*.json is tracked in git (was gitignored). The write path (write_decision_drop.py, iterate F3) has no gitleaks/prompt-scan hook, unlike other tracked artifact writers. Flagged by code-reviewer during that run's Stage 2 review as a non-blocking follow-up. Consider whether the existing pre-commit/CI scanner chain already covers newly-tracked files generically, or whether a dedicated check is needed for agent-authored JSON content landing in git.

title: Plan-reviewer model is unconfigurable in both /shipwright-plan and /shipwright-iterate; wire a plan_review role
detail:
AUTONOMOUS: yes.

CORRECTS a wrong dismissal. trg-cb2b8cb9 (the config half of the original ask) was dismissed 2026-08-07 as duplicating trg-88621183, reasoning 'already lists opus-plan-reviewer under the review role'. VERIFIED 2026-08-08 that this does not hold in the shipped code: grep -rn opus-plan-reviewer over shared/scripts/lib/model_tier_config.py + shared/scripts/tools/resolve_model_tier.py returns nothing, and plugins/shipwright-plan/ has zero references to the resolver (PR #599 wired /shipwright-iterate and /shipwright-build only). opus-plan-reviewer's model stays hardcoded via its own frontmatter (model: opus) and is immune to the flag/config mechanism the rest of the review cascade now has.

SCOPE:
1. Add a dedicated plan_review role to model_tier_config.py's ROLES / model_config.schema.json / resolve_model_tier.py CLI -- NOT the existing review role: this repo's own shipwright_model_config.json already pins review: sonnet, so reusing that role would silently downgrade the internal plan reviewer (today hardcoded opus) instead of making it configurable. plan_review gets its own independent dial, same flag > project config > unset(inherit) precedence, no shipped default that pins a tier for consumers (per trg-88621183's own REJECTED section) -- so attaching a non-Anthropic model later (e.g. Codex) is a config change, not a code change.
2. Wire /shipwright-plan Step 5-int's opus-plan-reviewer spawn (step-5-external-review.md, iterate-2026-08-07-plan-reviewer-wiring) to resolve plan_review and pass the resolved tier as the Agent tool's model= param, instead of relying solely on the agent's own frontmatter.
3. /shipwright-iterate has the SAME asymmetry independently: its own mini-plan review (iteration-planning.md, external_review.py --mode iterate) has no internal reviewer arm at all -- external-only with a Self-Review Fallback when unavailable, exactly the gap Step 5 had before iterate-2026-08-07-plan-reviewer-wiring. title: TC3.2a (auto, serial) Four skills still mandate a full read of decision_log.md although the index exists, and new ADR numbers collide
detail:
AUTONOMOUS: yes. SERIAL: run in TC3.2's slot, after TC3.1 merges. It edits
`context-loading.md`, which TC3.1 also touches and TC3.2 will touch — see OVERLAP below.

TWO defects, same surface, verified against the code on 2026-08-08 (main at #602).

=== DEFECT 1: the index was built and nothing reads it ===

`.shipwright/agent_docs/decision_log_index.md` exists and is well made: 331 lines
against decision_log.md's 4,379 (13x compression), two producers
(`write_decision_log.py` and `aggregate_decisions.py`), a drift guard
(`shared/tests/test_decision_log_index_producers.py::test_committed_index_is_not_stale`),
`hooks-and-pipeline.md` rows, and changelog staging.

A grep over `plugins/` finds ZERO readers. Only producers, staging and docs. Meanwhile
FOUR skills still mandate reading the whole source file:

  1. plugins/shipwright-iterate/skills/iterate/references/context-loading.md:11
     "decision_log.md - ALL architectural decisions (read completely)"
  2. plugins/shipwright-build/skills/build/references/first-actions.md:63
     "ALL architectural decisions (read the complete file)"
  3. plugins/shipwright-plan/skills/plan/references/first-actions.md:103
     "ALL architectural decisions (read the complete file)"
  4. plugins/shipwright-project/skills/project/references/step-1-interview.md:16
     "ALL past architectural decisions (read completely)"

THE MANDATE IS ALREADY BROKEN, SILENTLY. A single Read returns at most 2,000 lines.
decision_log.md is 4,379. Every one of those four instructions has been half-honoured
for as long as the file has been over the cap, with nothing reporting it. This is not a
future risk; it is the current state.

SCOPE: switch all four to index-first, detail-on-demand — read
`decision_log_index.md`, then read only the entries the change touches. The index
already carries a derived `current-status` (`- superseded by ADR-NNN`, derived from a
`(supersedes ADR-NNN)` marker rather than the sparse `**Status**` field), so relevance
is decidable from the index alone.

Do NOT simply delete the word "completely" — that trades a broken guarantee for no
guarantee. The replacement must name the index, say what triggers reading a full entry,
and stay honest about what is not read.

CHECK, do not assume: whether `shared/templates/` ships any of these instructions to
adopted projects (the gitignore template shipped the drops bug that way), and whether
`agents/section-builder.md:355` and the design/deploy/adopt mentions are writers rather
than readers — the grep suggests they are, but that was a grep, not a read.

=== DEFECT 2: five ADRs are all numbered 127 ===

Straight out of the generated `.shipwright/planning/adr/INDEX.md`:

  ADR-127 - Per-role model tiers for spawned subagents      127-agent-model-tiers-per-role-tiers.md
  ADR-127 - Bloat exception, atomic_write.py raised to 324  127-bloat-exception-atomic-write-....md
  ADR-127 - Decision-log and decision-drops indexes         127-decision-log-drops-index.md
  ADR-127 - Backfill events-context selection keys          127-events-context-backfill-keys.md
  ADR-127 - Run-id pointer lifecycle                        127-run-id-lifecycle-fixes.md

And it is not only 127: 097, 120, 125 and 126 are each duplicated too. 13 files on 5
numbers.

CAUSE: the number lives in the filename, and `get_next_adr_number` derives it by reading
`decision_log.md`. Five iterates branching off the same base all read "next = 127" and
all claimed it. Keeping the release-time fold serialized protects the numbering inside
`decision_log.md` — it does nothing for the per-iterate ADR spec filenames. Ten parallel
iterates in one night is what surfaced this; at one iterate at a time it effectively
could not happen.

FIX THE CAUSE, NOT THE HISTORY. Retroactive renumbering is the dangerous half:
ADR-097 is cited in 10 files, ADR-120 in 16, ADR-125 in 8. Those citations are ALREADY
ambiguous ("see ADR-120" resolves to two different decisions), and renaming breaks them.
So:
  a) Make collision impossible for new ADRs — allocate under the same lock the fold
     uses, or make the branch-side name provisional and resolve it at fold time. Pick
     one and write down why in the ADR.
  b) Add a test that FAILS on a duplicate number, so this cannot come back silently.
     There is none today, which is why five accumulated unnoticed.
  c) For the 13 existing files: REPORT them and propose a resolution. Do not rename in
     this iterate. Count the citations per number, state what a rename would break, and
     leave the decision to the operator. A wrong rename is worse than a known collision.

=== OVERLAP, read before starting ===

`context-loading.md` is contested. TC3.1 (`trg-e13567b8`, running now) adds the decision
drops to Layer 1 and edits the same list. TC3.2 (`trg-c0d83dce`) reports a truncated
mandated load and edits the same list. There is no merge queue.

Therefore: start only after TC3.1 has MERGED, and rebase onto it rather than onto the
base it branched from. When TC3.2 runs afterwards, it inherits the switched instruction
and only has to add the truncation report — say so in the ADR so TC3.2 does not
re-litigate the wording.

=== WHY THIS IS THE HIGH-VALUE HALF ===

The measured cost equation is calls x context: every call re-pays the whole accumulated
context. A 4,379-line file in Layer 1 of four different skills is paid for on every
single call of every run that loads it. 331 lines instead of 4,379 is a 13x cut on a
mandatory input — and it makes an instruction that is currently impossible to follow
actually followable. The index existing without a reader delivers none of that.
